description_full: Vår Energi ASA operates as an independent upstream oil and gas company on the Norwegian continental shelf in Norway. The company produces crude oil and natural gas liquids. It also engages in the production, development, and exploration assets on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS). The company was formerly known as Eni Norge AS and changed its name to Vår Energi AS in December 2018. The company was incorporated in 1965 and is headquartered in Sandnes, Norway. Vår Energi ASA is a subsidiary of Eni International B.V.

financial_summary: Var Energi ASA is a large-cap energy business with a $14.3B market cap on $8.0B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are contracting by -8.9pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 41% against a 8% cost of capital — a 33-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 59% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.7B in free cash flow — roughly 21 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.44× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -14.4% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 24× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 8.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and within its sector the business captures 4.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 44% operating margin runs 28pp above the Energy median (16%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 4.05x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.8% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 202 companies in the universe; the top four hold 40% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 88% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 67% and a beta of 0.51, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $25K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
val: The stock trades 36% below its DCF fair value of $17.87, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 87%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $12.51 to $26.50 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Energy peers: P/E 9.9 vs 13.4, EV/EBITDA 1.7 vs 6.9 and P/FCF 8.5 vs 14.3 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 11.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 20.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 0.7% annual cash-flow growth, 6pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 41% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 33pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.49).
It runs a 59% gross margin and converts 21% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-14.4% of assets).
ROE of 151% is amplified by 46.7x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.9x net debt to EBITDA ($683.6M of cash against $6.2B of debt), with interest covered 23.7x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.03 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The value-trap profile is elevated (54/100); see the breakdown below.
The current ratio of 0.61 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -6.6% over 3 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
own: It returns 8.2% a year to shareholders (8.8% in dividends).
people: With about 1,433 employees, each generates about $5.6M of revenue, 2.7x the Energy median.
That works out to $1.2M of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (0x revenue per employee).
